title: Thirteen Years in the Wrong Direction
book: The Silk Roads: A New History of the World
author: Peter Frankopan
wiifm: Yesterday Rome was the centre of the world. Today it is a rich customer at the far western end of somebody else's network, with a balance-of-payments problem. Frankopan's argument is that the last five hundred years of Western centrality are the anomaly and the two thousand years before them were the normal condition. The way in is the life of one Chinese envoy who was sent to make a military alliance, failed completely, lost thirteen years and ninety-seven men, and accidentally opened the most important trade system in human history.

ch.h: The man sent to buy an alliance
b: In 138 BC the Han court had a security problem. The Xiongnu, a confederation of horse nomads to the north, were raiding at will and could not be beaten in open country. The Emperor Wu's plan was diplomatic: somewhere far to the west lived the Yuezhi, a people the Xiongnu had driven out and humiliated. Find them, and you would have an ally with a grievance.

The man given the job was a palace attendant named Zhang Qian. He set out with a party of about a hundred, guided by a captured Xiongnu man called Ganfu, heading into territory of which the Chinese court had essentially no reliable knowledge.

He was intercepted almost immediately and held by the Xiongnu for about ten years. Not in a cell, he was treated as a valuable man, married a Xiongnu woman, had a son by her, and earned the confidence of the Xiongnu leader. Ten years is a large part of an adult working life. He could have stopped there, and nobody in China would ever have known.
Then he escaped, with Ganfu and his family, and continued west on the original mission.
ch.cap: Ten years captive, Zhang Qian still holds the envoy's staff

b: He reached Dayuan, Ferghana, in what is now Uzbekistan, and then the Yuezhi themselves, spending about a year among them and in Bactrian territory. And the mission failed, completely and finally. The Yuezhi had settled into a comfortable, prosperous country and had no interest whatever in a war of revenge thousands of miles to the east.

Zhang turned for home along the southern rim of the Tarim Basin, was captured by the Xiongnu a second time, was spared, and escaped again a year or so later when their leader died and the succession turned violent. He reached the Han capital in 126 or 125 BC, depending on the source. Of the hundred-odd men who had set out, he and Ganfu were the two who came back.

Measured against its objective, this is one of the most comprehensive diplomatic failures on record: thirteen years away, ten of them in captivity, ninety-seven men lost, no alliance. What he actually brought home was something nobody had sent him for, intelligence. There were sophisticated, wealthy, literate states out there that China had not known existed: Ferghana, Bactria, Parthia, and beyond them rumours of more. He brought alfalfa seed. And he brought word of horses in Ferghana, taller and faster than anything in China, which the Chinese would call heavenly horses and would eventually go to war to obtain.

There was one more detail in his report, and Frankopan's whole book hangs on it. In the markets of Bactria, Zhang saw bamboo canes and cloth from Shu, the region of modern Sichuan in China's south-west. He asked how they had got there and was told that merchants bought them in India. Chinese goods were already reaching Central Asia by a route the Chinese court had never heard of. The network existed before the empire went looking for it.

Frankopan's first structural point sits here. The network was not opened for silk, or for luxury, or by merchants. It was opened by a defence problem and consolidated by a military requirement. Trade routes are usually a by-product of somebody's security policy.
ch.cap: In Bactria, Zhang Qian finds Sichuan bamboo for sale

b: Zhang Qian's report changed what the Han court wanted. The Emperor Wu became fixed on the horses of Ferghana, the ones said to sweat blood, and sent envoys with gold, including a horse made of gold, to buy some. The king of Dayuan refused. The chief envoy lost his temper, smashed the golden horse, and was killed on the road home.

In 104 BC Wu sent an army under the general Li Guangli more than two thousand miles across desert and mountains to take the horses by force. It ran out of food, fought its way to the edge of Ferghana and limped back. The emperor ordered the survivors to stay outside the Jade Gate rather than come home in disgrace, and raised a far larger army, said to number sixty thousand men, with tens of thousands of oxen, horses and donkeys to carry supplies. After a siege of the capital of Dayuan in 101 BC, the city's nobles killed their own king and handed over the horses. The army came home with a few thousand animals, and far fewer survived the march.

Weigh the cost against the yield and it looks absurd, a vast army for a herd of horses. But the campaign did what Zhang's journey had not. It showed the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin that Chinese power could reach them, and the Han built garrisons, watchtowers and supply stations along the Gansu corridor out towards Dunhuang. Those forts and wells made the routes safe enough for merchants, and silk flowed west partly as soldiers' pay and as gifts to the peoples whose cooperation the frontier needed.
Frankopan's point is that this is how infrastructure usually gets built. A state pays for it for its own strategic reasons, commerce moves in afterwards, and the commerce outlives the reasons.
ch.cap: Dayuan's gate opens and the heavenly horses come out

b: Now meet the man who chose to tell this story. Peter Frankopan was born in London in 1971, into a family of Croatian descent, and in the preface to The Silk Roads he recalls that one of his most treasured possessions as a boy was a large map of the world. What puzzled him, he says, was how much of it his history lessons ignored. The story he was taught ran from Greece to Rome to Christian Europe to the modern West, and the enormous space between the Mediterranean and China, Persia, Mesopotamia and the steppe, appeared only when it attacked somebody.

He became an Oxford historian of Byzantium, the eastern Roman empire that Gibbon had treated with such impatience, and spent years with its sources, including editing a new edition of the Alexiad, the history written by the Byzantine princess Anna Komnene about her father's reign. Byzantium is good training for this argument, because from Constantinople the world never looked as if it centred on Western Europe. It looked as if it centred on the corridors running east.

The Silk Roads, published in 2015, was his attempt to turn the map round. The subtitle, A New History of the World, is a deliberate provocation. The claim is that the lands running from the eastern Mediterranean to the Himalayas, which Western narratives treat as a hinterland, were for most of recorded history the centre of the world: where empires were made, religions were born and money was concentrated. The book became an international bestseller, which tells you how many readers had sat through the same lessons.
ch.cap: Young Frankopan's finger finds the map's forgotten middle

ch.h: There was never a Silk Road
b: Dismantle the phrase before you use it again. The term Seidenstrasse was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, uncle of the flying ace, and it names a scholarly abstraction, not a road.

What existed was a shifting mesh of routes, overland and maritime and riverine, linking China, India, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean. Nobody in the ancient world used the word. Nobody travelled the whole length of it. Goods did, passing through dozens of hands, each taking a margin, which is precisely why a bolt of Chinese silk cost a Roman senator a fortune and the weaver who made it almost nothing.

That margin structure is the whole commercial lesson. Value in a long chain does not accrue to whoever makes the thing or whoever wants it. It accrues to whoever controls a segment that cannot be routed around.
ch.cap: Silk passes through many hands, each taking a cut

b: In 1907 the archaeologist Aurel Stein was working along the old Chinese frontier when he opened a ruined watchtower west of Dunhuang, near the Jade Gate. Inside was a bundle of letters, written on paper in Sogdian, the language of Central Asian merchants. They had been posted around 313 AD and had never reached anyone, confiscated, or abandoned, and had lain in the sand of the Gobi for sixteen centuries.

One is the most human document to survive from the trade routes. A merchant named Nanai-dhat had gone east on business and left his wife, Miwnay, and his daughter, Shayn, stranded in Dunhuang with no money. After three years of being told to wait, Miwnay sent her husband a letter, and its most famous line, in Nicholas Sims-Williams's translation, needs no literary training to improve it: “I would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than yours!”

Keep that in your head, because it tells you what these routes actually were. Not a romantic corridor of caravans and lacquer boxes. A commercial system with credit, debt, remittance failure, abandoned dependants and furious women, the same system you would recognise if you ran an import business, operating across four thousand miles and several empires, in the fourth century.
ch.cap: Stein lifts lost merchant letters from a Gobi watchtower

b: Now put Gibbon's empire back on the map and watch it change shape.

Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century AD, complained that India, China and Arabia were draining the empire of a hundred million sesterces a year to pay for luxuries, silk, pepper, pearls, incense. Scholars argue about whether he exaggerated, and the archaeology does not obviously contradict him: hoards of Roman gold and silver coin from the first and second centuries turn up in southern India, and under Augustus Roman ships were running from Red Sea ports to the Indian coast on the monsoon winds.

Consider what that means. The most powerful state in the western world was running a structural deficit with Asia to buy things it could not make, and settling in hard metal, because it had nothing Asia wanted in exchange. Rome was not the hub. Rome was the wealthy terminal customer, and the terms were set elsewhere.

If that arrangement sounds familiar, that is Frankopan's point, made quietly. The centuries in which Europe and then North America sat at the centre of the world economy are a recent interruption in a much longer pattern.
ch.cap: Roman gold sails east on the monsoon for silk

b: The second cargo was religion, and it moved in directions that will surprise anyone taught history in a European classroom.

Buddhism began in northern India and travelled north-west along the trade routes into Central Asia, then east into China, carried by merchants, not armies. The cave complexes at Dunhuang and Bamiyan were funded by traders buying merit. Christianity ran the same way: Frankopan traces communities in Yemen, on Socotra, in Sri Lanka, and eventually in Tang China, where a stone stele erected in 781 records a church in the capital.

For most of the first millennium the geographical centre of gravity of Christianity was not in Europe at all. It was in the Middle East and running east. The faith that Europeans would later carry to the world as their own possession had already been an Asian religion for centuries, and had travelled on the same credit networks as the pepper.
The transferable observation: ideas move along the channels built for commerce, at commerce's speed, and they move where the margin is, not where the argument is strongest.
ch.cap: Monks follow the caravans to the Dunhuang caves

ch.h: The network does not care who is emperor
b: This is the structural claim that makes the book more than a corrective to Eurocentrism, and it is the reason it is on this week's list between Gibbon and Tuchman.

Empires rose and fell at the nodes. The network persisted. Han China collapsed; the routes carried on. Rome fell in the west; the routes carried on. The Sasanians were destroyed by the Arab conquests; the routes not only carried on but thickened, because the new caliphates sat astride them and had every interest in traffic. Nodes are mortal. Networks are not, or at least not on the same clock.

The pattern repeats down the centuries. In the thirteenth century the Mongols, the most destructive conquerors in the book, built the largest land empire in history and then made it, for a time, one of the safest places in the world to move goods. The same connections carried the Black Death, which came off the steppe to the Crimea and from there by ship into the Mediterranean in 1347, killing perhaps a third of Europe's population or more. Then, at the end of the fifteenth century, Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492 and Vasco da Gama sailed round Africa to India in 1498, and the centre of gravity began to move. Europe had not out-competed the old routes. It had found a way round them, and the silver of the Americas paid for its entry into Asian trade.

So when you ask why something large fell over, Frankopan's question is a different one from Gibbon's. Gibbon looks inside the institution for the load. Frankopan asks what the institution was a node on, who else was on it, and whether the traffic simply rerouted.

Both questions are worth having. Yesterday's book tells you how a thing dies from the inside. Today's tells you that its death may be close to irrelevant to the system it belonged to, and that if you want to understand durability, you should study the road rather than the city.
ch.cap: The caravan walks on past the ruins of empires

ch.h: Where to be careful with this book
b: Read it with two reservations, because it is an argument as well as a history.

The first is that the frame can flatten. By running from antiquity to the present day across the whole of Eurasia in one volume, Frankopan necessarily compresses, and specialists have objected that the Silk Roads label gets stretched to cover almost any east-west contact, including, in the later chapters, twentieth-century oil and Cold War politics, where the continuity with Sogdian letter-writers becomes more rhetorical than real. A unifying thesis that explains two thousand years of everything explains slightly less than it appears to.

The second is a caution against over-correcting. The book is a necessary answer to a European story that treated Asia as a periphery, but the answer is not that Europe never mattered. The five centuries from around 1500 were a real and consequential reordering, not an illusion, and some of Frankopan's rhetorical weight is spent making them sound more temporary than the evidence quite supports.

Notice, too, when the book appeared. In 2013 China's president, Xi Jinping, announced what became known as the Belt and Road Initiative, a programme of ports, railways and pipelines across Eurasia openly branded as a new Silk Road. Frankopan's history arrived two years later and was read partly as a guide to the present, and in 2018 he published a short sequel, The New Silk Roads. That relevance is a strength, and also a reason to ask whether the past is being shaped to fit the present.

What survives both objections is the method. Before you explain why something declined, establish what network it sat on and who else was on it, because the most important fact about any node is usually not inside it.
ch.cap: A historian weighs ancient routes against a modern slogan

take: Trade routes are a by-product of defence policy

Zhang Qian was sent in 138 BC to buy a military alliance, not to open commerce. The network followed from a security problem and a hunger for Ferghana horses. Ask what somebody's strategic anxiety is currently building, because that is where the next commercial channel appears.
Total failure can be the most valuable outcome

Thirteen years away, ten of them captive, ninety-seven men lost, no alliance, and the intelligence he brought back reorganised Chinese foreign policy and opened Eurasia. Judge an expedition by what it taught you, not only by whether it achieved its stated objective.
There was no road, only a mesh
Nobody travelled the whole length and nobody used the name until 1877. Goods passed through dozens of hands, each taking a cut, which is why silk cost a senator a fortune and its weaver nothing.

Value accrues not to the maker or the buyer but to whoever controls a segment nobody can route around. Count the real alternatives to each of your five biggest suppliers; where the answer is one, someone else sets your price.
Know whether you are the hub or the customer

Rome ran a structural deficit with Asia, paying in hard metal for things it could not make. Most small businesses sit further down the chain than they believe, and the first step is to establish honestly which end you are on.

Buddhism and Christianity both moved east along the trade routes, carried by merchants and funded by traders buying merit. Influence spreads where the traffic and the margin already are, not where the argument is best.
Nodes are mortal, networks are not
Han China fell, Rome fell, the Sasanians were destroyed, and the routes carried on, in some cases thickening. Before diagnosing a collapse from the inside, ask whether the traffic simply rerouted.
Distrust a thesis that explains everything

Stretching the Silk Roads frame to cover Cold War oil politics makes the continuity rhetorical rather than real. Take the method, map the network first, and hold the grand unifying claim more loosely.
recall: What was Zhang Qian actually sent to do, and what did he deliver?

He was sent west in 138 BC by Emperor Wu to recruit the Yuezhi into a military alliance against the Xiongnu. The Yuezhi refused. He delivered intelligence instead: the existence of wealthy literate states to the west, alfalfa seed, and word of the Ferghana horses, which reoriented Han policy and opened the routes.
Why is the phrase “Silk Road” misleading?

It was coined in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen and names a scholarly abstraction, not a road. What existed was a shifting mesh of overland, maritime and riverine routes; nobody travelled its full length, and goods passed through dozens of intermediaries each taking a margin.
How does Frankopan's question differ from Gibbon's?

Gibbon looks inside an institution for the load that brought it down. Frankopan asks what network the institution was a node on, who else was on it, and whether the traffic simply rerouted after it fell, because nodes are mortal and networks largely are not.
Why did the Han go to war with Ferghana, and what did the campaign actually build?

The Emperor Wu wanted Ferghana's heavenly horses, and when his envoy was refused and killed he sent Li Guangli west in 104 BC, then again with a much larger army until Dayuan surrendered its horses in 101 BC. The lasting result was a chain of Han garrisons, watchtowers and supply stations along the Gansu corridor that made the routes safe for merchants.
What did Zhang Qian see in Bactria, and why does it matter to Frankopan?

He saw bamboo and cloth from Sichuan that had reached Bactria through India, by a route the Han court knew nothing about. It shows that the trading network existed before any empire set out to open it, which is Frankopan's argument that networks are older and tougher than the states sitting on them.
note: Frankopan is a living academic historian, so the biographical chapter rests on his own account in the book's preface and on his published career (Oxford Byzantinist, editor of the Penguin Alexiad, The Silk Roads 2015, The New Silk Roads 2018). Zhang Qian's mission is as recorded by Sima Qian and summarised in modern scholarship: a party of about a hundred, about ten years' detention within a thirteen-year absence, two survivors; sources disagree on whether he returned in 126 or 125 BC. The Ferghana campaigns of 104 to 101 BC and the Sichuan goods in Bactria also come from Sima Qian, whose army sizes are traditional figures. Stein's 1907 find near the Jade Gate and the Sogdian Ancient Letters follow Nicholas Sims-Williams's translation; the letters' date of about 313 is the usual but not unanimous one. Pliny's hundred-million-sesterces figure is his own claim and is disputed.
words: Profiting from the difference in price for the same thing in two different markets.
Silk was cheap where it was woven and a fortune in Rome, and every intermediary along the routes lived on a slice of that gap.
The remote region lying behind a coast, a city or a centre of attention, treated as secondary to it.
Frankopan's complaint is that Western history treats the lands between the Mediterranean and China as a hinterland when for most of history they were the centre.
Money in the form of coins of gold or silver, as opposed to paper or credit.
Rome paid for Asian silk and pepper in specie, which is why hoards of Roman coin turn up in southern India.
An upright stone slab carved with an inscription, used as a monument or public record.
A stele erected in 781 records a Christian church in the capital of Tang China.
A trading hub where goods are brought in, bought, sold and sent on rather than consumed.
The markets of Bactria acted as an entrepôt, which is where Zhang Qian found cloth from Sichuan that had travelled by way of India.
stories: The most useful failure in history

In 138 BC the Han emperor sent a palace attendant called Zhang Qian west to recruit the Yuezhi as allies against the nomad Xiongnu. He was captured almost at once and held for about ten years, long enough to marry and have a son. He escaped, kept going, found the Yuezhi, and discovered they had settled somewhere comfortable and had no interest in a war. On the way home he was captured again. Of roughly a hundred men who set out, two came back, thirteen years later. No alliance. But he brought home something nobody had sent him for: news of rich kingdoms in the west and of wonderful horses. That report opened the Silk Roads.

In 1907 the archaeologist Aurel Stein opened a ruined watchtower near the Jade Gate, west of Dunhuang, and found a bundle of letters that had never been delivered. They were written in Sogdian, the language of Central Asian merchants, around 313 AD. One was from a woman called Miwnay. Her merchant husband, Nanai-dhat, had gone east on business and left her and their daughter stranded with no money. After three years of being told to wait, she wrote to tell him exactly what she thought, and in Nicholas Sims-Williams's translation it still lands: “I would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than yours!” The romance of the Silk Road came with unpaid bills.

Zhang Qian's report left the Emperor Wu obsessed with the horses of Ferghana, said to sweat blood. He sent envoys with gold, including a horse made of gold, to buy some. The king of Dayuan refused. The chief envoy lost his temper, smashed the golden horse, and was killed on the road home. So Wu sent an army across desert and mountains. It ran out of food and limped back, and the emperor would not let the survivors through the Jade Gate. A second army, traditionally said to number sixty thousand, besieged the city until its own nobles killed their king and handed over the horses. The forts built along the way made the routes safe for merchants.
biz: Own a segment nobody can route around

On the Silk Roads the profit went to whoever held a stretch nobody could bypass. A secured-loan broker sits between platforms that own the traffic and lenders that own the money, and can be squeezed from both sides. The segment you can own is trust: homeowners who find you through your own SEO pages, a fact-find careful enough that lenders value your referrals, and customers who recommend you. This week, make sure every enquiry is tagged with its true source, and track monthly what share comes from owned channels rather than paid clicks. If paid is above four in five, the platforms are setting your price.
Treat every decline as a returning envoy

Zhang Qian failed his mission and came back with intelligence that reshaped Chinese policy. Every application that does not proceed is a small failed expedition. Start logging, for each one, the lender, the customer's broad circumstances and the stated reason. Within a few weeks you will see which lenders reliably decline which situations, so you stop putting customers through applications unlikely to succeed. That is fairer to the customer under Consumer Duty, saves hours of work, and protects your standing with lenders. Review the log monthly and update how you match customers to lenders.
connects: Adam Smith attacked the old fear that paying out gold and silver for imports makes a nation poorer, the same worry Pliny voiced about Rome's bill for silk.
Thiel's argument that profit flows to whoever holds a position others cannot copy is Frankopan's point that margin accrues at the chokepoint nobody can route around.
Meadows's habit of studying the structure of a system rather than its parts matches Frankopan's claim that cities rise and fall while the network carries on.
recap:
About a hundred and thirty-eight years before the birth of Christ, the emperor of Han China had a problem. Nomad horsemen called the Xiongnu were raiding his borders and could not be beaten. So he sent a palace attendant called Zhang Qian into the unknown west to find an ally. Zhang was captured almost at once and held for about ten years. He married, had a son, escaped, kept going, found the people he was looking for, and learned they had no interest in a war. He was captured again on the way home. Thirteen years after he left, he and one companion were the only survivors of about a hundred men.

The mission failed completely, and yet what he brought back changed the world. He reported rich, literate kingdoms nobody in China had heard of, magnificent horses, and, in the markets of Bactria, cloth from south-west China that had got there by a route the court never knew existed. The network was already there before the empire went looking for it.

Two thousand years later a London schoolboy called Peter Frankopan stared at his map of the world and wondered why his history lessons ignored most of it. He became an Oxford historian of Byzantium, and in twenty fifteen he published The Silk Roads to turn the map round.

His first idea is that trade routes are usually a side effect of somebody's security policy. The Chinese built forts and wells to get horses and hold the frontier, and merchants moved in behind the soldiers.

His second is that there was never a single Silk Road. The phrase was coined by a German geographer in eighteen seventy-seven. What existed was a mesh of routes, and goods passed through dozens of hands, each taking a cut. The profit went to whoever controlled a stretch nobody could bypass.

His third is that Rome was not the centre of the world. It was a wealthy customer at the far end of somebody else's network, paying for silk and pepper in gold and silver because it had little that Asia wanted.

His fourth is that ideas travel along the channels built for trade. Buddhism and Christianity both moved east with the merchants.

And his fifth is the deepest. Empires rise and fall at the junctions, but the network carries on. Han China fell, Rome fell, and the traffic simply found another way.

Read him with some care, because a theory that explains two thousand years of everything can stretch too far, and specialists say it sometimes does. But keep the method.

The line to remember is this. The most important fact about any city is usually the road that runs through it.
